opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I found it pretty unsatisfying. This was back when I was an undergrad, and the AI class was very much in the good old-fashioned style: search algorithms, logic, knowledge representation, hand-built rules for how a system should reason. You'd write out explicitly how the program should handle every situation, and it would follow those rules.

Coming at it as someone who was really drawn to physics, it felt almost the opposite of what I thought intelligence should be. It was very engineered, very brittle. You had to anticipate everything in advance, and if the world did something you hadn't encoded, the system just fell over. There wasn't any sense that the thing was *learning* or discovering structure on its own. It was more like elaborate bookkeeping.

In physics, what excites you is finding simple underlying principles that explain a huge range of phenomena. You don't write down a separate rule for every falling object; you find the law that governs all of them. GOFAI felt like the reverse: piling up special cases and hoping that, if you piled up enough, something intelligent would emerge. I didn't believe that was how brains worked, and I didn't find it intellectually compelling.

So I kind of walked away from AI for a while and went deep into physics, theoretical physics, quantum field theory. It was only later, when deep learning started working, that I came back. What drew me back was that these systems *learn* from data, and suddenly there was a real scientific question about why they work. That felt much more like a physics problem: a complicated system with lots of interacting parts, where you want to find the effective theory that describes its behavior. That was a very different feeling from the class, where it all just seemed like rules all the way down.

r001.rationale: He says deep learning drew him back to AI, but does not say ideas from his undergraduate class became relevant again.

r002.rationale: He describes the class’s rule-based AI as almost the opposite of intelligence and says he did not believe that was how brains worked.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I took an AI class as an undergrad, and honestly I came away pretty unimpressed. It was very much the old-school stuff: search algorithms, logic, planning, hand-coded rules. You'd write down a bunch of symbols and relations and then have the computer manipulate them. And it didn't feel like intelligence to me. It felt like clever engineering, where all the actual intelligence was coming from the person who wrote the rules.

I remember thinking, this is just brittle. The moment you step outside the world the programmer anticipated, the whole thing falls apart. And as a physics person, that was unsatisfying, because in physics you want a few principles that generalize. You don't want to enumerate every case by hand. So I basically wrote the field off. I thought, okay, this is interesting as computer science, but it's not going to tell me anything deep about what thinking actually is.

Which, in retrospect, is kind of funny, because the thing that eventually pulled me back in was the exact opposite approach. Neural networks, where you don't hand-code the knowledge at all. You set up a very simple system, scale it up, and let the structure emerge from the data. That felt much more like physics. Lots of simple components, collective behavior, and the interesting question is why the emergent thing looks the way it does. So I didn't change my mind about the good old-fashioned stuff. I just found the version of AI that spoke my language.

r001.rationale: He says he did not change his mind about the old-school approach; neural networks, which he describes as the opposite approach, brought him back to AI. He does not say the class’s ideas became relevant again.

r002.rationale: He says the rule-based systems in his class did not feel like intelligence and would not explain what thinking is, describing the intelligence as coming from the person who wrote the rules.

astra-6.text: I thought it was intellectually interesting, but it didn’t feel like intelligence to me. You were writing down rules and telling the computer how to reason within those rules. The cleverness seemed to be coming from the person designing the system, rather than from the system itself. I had a hard time seeing how that would get us to something that could learn and deal with the complexity of the real world.

r001.rationale: The response describes his reaction to the class but does not say those ideas are becoming relevant again.

sol-6.1.text: I thought it was fascinating, but it felt more like a collection of clever tricks than a path to intelligence. You’d specify the rules, choose a representation, and then search through the possibilities. It could work beautifully within the little world you’d defined, but so much of the intelligence seemed to be coming from the person setting up the problem. The part that really interested me was how a machine could learn those representations and rules for itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes how the class’s AI worked and what interested Dan, but does not say those ideas are becoming relevant again.

r002.rationale: Calling the material “a collection of clever tricks” rather than “a path to intelligence,” and saying much of the intelligence came from the person setting up the problem, communicates a disconnect between the algorithms taught and intelligence.
